title: AI-Assisted Product Delivery: A Growth Leader's Playbook
excerpt: A practical guide to AI-assisted product delivery: define the workflow, control scope, verify generated work and hand over a product teams can use.
body:
![Editorial illustration of AI-assisted product assembly moving through requirements and a verification gate.](/media/blogs/ai-assisted-product-delivery.webp)

*From a defined workflow to a verified product increment. AI-generated editorial illustration.*

Generating a working screen is increasingly easy. Knowing whether it represents the right workflow, respects the right permissions and can be supported after release remains demanding work.

That distinction matters for growth and operations leaders using AI to build internal tools. Faster code generation can shorten an implementation step while leaving the underlying business problem unresolved.

My role in AI-assisted delivery has included defining requirements, making product decisions, correcting behaviour, running builds and checks, reviewing interfaces and preparing handovers. It is important to describe that role accurately: product ownership and delivery direction are not the same as claiming sole manual authorship of every line of code.

**The value of AI-assisted product delivery depends on the quality of the decisions and verification around the generated work.** This is the playbook I would use to turn an operating problem into a reviewable, maintainable product increment.

## Begin with a workflow that is currently failing

“Build a CRM dashboard” is a solution request. “Managers cannot identify overdue callbacks without opening several spreadsheets” is a problem statement.

The second gives the team a user, a task, an obstacle and a possible outcome. It also allows several solutions: a better existing view, a small report or a new interface. Starting with a tool name can commit the organisation to unnecessary scope.

I would collect a few representative examples of the failed workflow, including its exceptions. Use synthetic or appropriately sanitised records for development rather than copying live personal information into prompts or test fixtures.

Then define the first useful outcome in observable terms: an authorised manager can find overdue callbacks for their branch, understand the next action and open the relevant record. That is a more productive brief than “make it professional and feature-rich.”

## Write down the invariants before the interface

An invariant is a condition that must remain true as the product changes.

For an operations tool, examples might include: a branch user cannot read another branch's records; each valid enquiry keeps its original source identifier; a sync retry does not create a duplicate; and a clinical or billing system remains the authority for its own records.

These statements guide architecture, implementation and tests. They also help review AI-generated changes that look plausible but alter the operating model.

I would keep the first specification short enough to use: the user journey, required fields, permission boundaries, data ownership, failure states and acceptance criteria. A large document that nobody checks is less useful than a precise page used at every review.

## Give AI a bounded task with a visible finish line

Broad requests encourage broad, difficult-to-review changes. A bounded task might be: “Add an authorised branch filter to this existing report, preserve its current layout and verify that users cannot retrieve records outside their membership.”

The task should name the relevant context and the constraints that matter. It should also specify what evidence would establish completion.

For a contact form, for example, the finish line may include required-field validation, duplicate-submission handling, a clear success state and confirmed delivery to the intended backend. A rendered form alone would satisfy only the visual part of the task.

I would review one coherent increment at a time. Smaller changes make it easier to identify which decision caused a problem and to revert an implementation without discarding unrelated work.

## Treat the generated explanation as a claim to verify

An assistant can explain code fluently and still miss a permission failure, an edge case or a framework constraint. GitHub's responsible-use guidance similarly emphasises human review and validation of agent output. See [GitHub's guidance for Copilot agents](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/responsible-use/agents).

That is a general engineering principle, not an endorsement of one particular tool or a statement about the tools used in every project I have delivered.

I would inspect the actual change and ask the system to demonstrate the behaviour. If it says a form writes to a sheet, examine the authorised test result. If it says branch access is restricted, test a prohibited request. If it says a deployment succeeded, open the routes that users will actually visit.

Verification should follow the claim rather than the confidence of the explanation.

## Use a ladder of delivery evidence

Different checks prove different things:

| Evidence | What it supports | What it does not establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type checking and a successful build | Code can pass those configured checks | Correct business behaviour |
| Focused automated tests | Specific tested rules behave as expected | Every integration and user journey works |
| Local interface review | The tested screen behaves in that environment | Production configuration is correct |
| Deployed route and permission checks | Particular live paths and boundaries work | Sustained reliability over time |
| Authorised end-to-end transaction | The tested workflow reaches its intended destination | All future transactions will succeed |
| Operating observation after release | Behaviour across real usage and time | Permanent freedom from defects |

The purpose of the ladder is to make completion statements precise. “The build passed” is a useful fact. “The product is fully ready” requires a wider body of evidence.

This distinction has been especially important in work involving web previews, Android builds, CRM synchronisation and content-management authentication. Each environment can pass one check while still lacking another part of the user journey.

## Ask operations to review realistic scenarios

The best interface review is not a tour of all the buttons. It is a person trying to complete a recognisable task.

I would ask a manager to find a missed commitment, an executive to record an unsuccessful visit and an administrator to investigate a failed sync. Include incomplete information and ordinary mistakes. Those scenarios reveal whether the product supports the work or merely the ideal path in the specification.

Record the difference between a preference and a defect. A button label may be a usability improvement; access to another branch's records is a permission defect. The response and release priority should reflect that difference.

When feedback changes the requirement, update the acceptance criteria. Otherwise, the team can keep testing the original brief while implementing a different product.

## Keep the architecture smaller than the ambition

An internal tool does not need every capability on its first release. It needs a coherent workflow, an understood source of truth and a way to recover when something fails.

I would choose one narrow operating problem, use existing systems where they fit and record the boundaries of the new tool. If the business already has a clinical or billing system, a growth application should not accidentally become a competing version of those records.

The DORA 2025 research describes AI as amplifying the strengths and weaknesses of the surrounding delivery system. That finding supports investing in clear requirements, review and feedback alongside generation speed. See the [DORA 2025 report](https://dora.dev/research/2025/dora-report/).

More generated code does not remove the cost of understanding, operating and changing it later.

## Make release and rollback part of the product brief

Before deployment, I would identify the target environment, required configuration, account ownership, migration effects and rollback path. A new environment variable or an external integration can make identical code behave differently in production.

Record the release version and the checks performed against it. If a new change follows, decide which evidence needs to be refreshed. A successful test against an older build is not proof of a later one.

The handover should explain how to recognise a healthy system and what to do when it is unhealthy. Include ordinary support tasks, not only installation instructions. Someone should be able to find the owner of a credential, inspect an error and pause a problematic workflow without reverse-engineering the entire project.

## Measure delivered usefulness

I would evaluate an AI-assisted project through task completion, error reduction, recovery effort, adoption and time spent on the original problem. Those measures need a baseline and a fair observation period.

Avoid claiming time savings merely because a tool was released. A team may still use the previous spreadsheet, or the new process may move work from one role to another. Watch the actual workflow before calculating the benefit.

For growth and operations leaders, the opportunity is substantial: people who understand the business can participate more directly in product delivery. The responsibility grows with that opportunity. Clear scope, honest evidence and operational ownership remain the foundations of a useful release.

My [FieldOps project](/projects/fieldops-healthcare-field-operations-platform) and [ANKURAM OS work](/projects/ankuram-os-revenue-operations) show this connection between business requirements and technology delivery. For roles that need that combination, visit my [experience page](/experience) or [contact me](/contact).
